## Ordinary differential equations — Day 1, Session 3

Worksheet: `worksheets/03-solving-odes-with-events.qmd`. The
chapter is [Ordinary differential
equations](../chapters/03-ordinary-differential-equations.qmd).

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch03-setup
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using DiffEqCallbacks
using CairoMakie

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I
    du[3] = p.γ * I
    return nothing
end

u0    = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
p     = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
tspan = (0.0, 80.0)
tt    = 0.0:0.25:80.0

sol = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5(); reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)

println("peak infectious: ", round(maximum(sol(t)[2] for t in tt), digits = 1))
println("final size (R at day 80): ", round(sol(80.0)[3], digits = 1))
```

### Part A — a vaccination pulse

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch03-a1
t_vax = 10.0     # day of the campaign
f_vax = 0.30     # fraction of susceptibles reached
vaccinated = Float64[]     # record of how many the campaign reached

function vaccinate!(integrator)
    moved = f_vax * integrator.u[1]
    integrator.u[1] -= moved
    integrator.u[3] += moved
    push!(vaccinated, moved)
end

vax_cb  = PresetTimeCallback([t_vax], vaccinate!)
sol_vax = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5();
                callback = vax_cb, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)

# R now holds recovered and vaccinated people alike, so the number ever infected
# is no longer just R(80) — subtract the people the campaign put there.
ever_infected = sol_vax(80.0)[3] - sum(vaccinated)
baseline_infected = sol(80.0)[3]
peak_vax = maximum(sol_vax(t)[2] for t in tt)
peak_base = maximum(sol(t)[2] for t in tt)

check("population still conserved",
      all(u -> isapprox(sum(u), 1000.0; atol = 1e-6), sol_vax.u))
check("the campaign moved people out of S", sum(vaccinated) > 1.0)
check("the peak is lower", peak_vax < 0.8 * peak_base)
check("fewer people were ever infected", ever_infected < baseline_infected - 50)

(; vaccinated = round(sum(vaccinated); digits = 1),
   peak_base = round(peak_base; digits = 1), peak_vax = round(peak_vax; digits = 1),
   ever_infected = round(ever_infected; digits = 1),
   baseline_infected = round(baseline_infected; digits = 1))
```

#### A1. Interpret

- The campaign reaches about 246 people on day 10. The peak falls from about 158
  to about 91, and the number ever infected from about 800 to about 498.
- $R(80)$ alone would have said 744 against a baseline of 800 — an improvement,
  but badly understated, and for a campaign late in the epidemic it flips sign
  and appears to make things *worse*.
- After a campaign $R$ no longer means "people who have been infected". It holds
  the recovered and the vaccinated together, answering "how many are immune now",
  and only the first of those measures burden. Subtracting `sum(vaccinated)`
  separates them again.
- A count rather than a rate shows as a step: the callback fires once, so $S$ and
  $R$ jump vertically at day 10 while $I$ is untouched at that instant, leaving no
  jump in the infectious curve.
- There is a corner, though. With $\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t = \lambda S - \gamma I$
  and $S$ down by 246, the growth rate drops from about 13.7 to about 3.2 people
  per day. It does not go negative — $S = 574$ is still above $N/R_0 = 500$ — so
  $I$ keeps rising for three more days and peaks on day 13 instead of day 17.5.
- A rate would have bent all three curves gradually, with no corner anywhere.
  Taking `moved` out of `u[1]` and adding the same quantity to `u[3]` is what
  keeps the population constant, and the conservation check is what confirms
  it.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch03-vax
#| fig-cap: "Infectious curve with and without a vaccination pulse on day 10."
fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax  = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)")
vlines!(ax, [t_vax]; color = :black, linestyle = :dot, label = "campaign")
lines!(ax, tt, [sol(t)[2] for t in tt]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3,
       label = "no vaccination")
lines!(ax, tt, [sol_vax(t)[2] for t in tt]; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 3,
       linestyle = :dash, label = "vaccination on day $(Int(t_vax))")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

### Part B — when should the campaign happen?

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch03-b1
function ever_infected_with_vaccination(day)
    moved_by_campaign = Float64[]
    affect!(integrator) = begin
        moved = f_vax * integrator.u[1]
        integrator.u[1] -= moved
        integrator.u[3] += moved
        push!(moved_by_campaign, moved)
    end
    s = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5();
              callback = PresetTimeCallback([day], affect!),
              reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
    return s(80.0)[3] - sum(moved_by_campaign)
end

campaign_days = [5.0, 20.0, 40.0]

for d in campaign_days
    println("campaign on day $d → $(round(ever_infected_with_vaccination(d), digits = 1)) ever infected")
end

check("three days tried", length(campaign_days) == 3)
```

#### B1. Interpret

- Day 5 is much the best: about 414 people ever infected, against about 708 for
  day 20 and about 796 for day 40 — the last barely better than the 800 with no
  campaign at all.
- The same 30% coverage protects a different number each time, because it is 30%
  *of whoever is still susceptible*. On day 5 that is almost the whole
  population, so the campaign removes a large block of fuel before the epidemic
  accelerates; by day 40 most people have already been infected, and those still
  susceptible were unlikely to be infected in the time remaining.
- Beyond protecting individuals, removing susceptibles early lowers the force of
  infection for everyone left behind, so each vaccination also prevents further
  infections indirectly. That is why acting early buys more than the difference
  in doses delivered would suggest.

### Part C — a lockdown that triggers itself

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch03-c1
capacity = 100.0
trigger_day = Float64[]

capacity_condition(u, t, integrator) = u[2] - capacity

function impose_restrictions!(integrator)
    integrator.p = merge(integrator.p, (β = 0.02,))     # β drops
    push!(trigger_day, integrator.t)
end

# the third argument, `nothing`, means "fire on the way up only"
cap_cb  = ContinuousCallback(capacity_condition, impose_restrictions!, nothing)
sol_cap = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5();
                callback = cap_cb, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)

check("the trigger fired", !isempty(trigger_day))
check("restrictions kept I near capacity",
      maximum(sol_cap(t)[2] for t in tt) < 1.1 * capacity)

isempty(trigger_day) || println("restrictions imposed on day ",
                                round(trigger_day[1], digits = 2))
```

#### C1. Interpret

- The trigger fires on day 11.0 and the infectious curve tops out at almost
  exactly the capacity of 100.
- The scheduled campaign in Part A requires knowing *when* to act, and so
  requires knowing in advance how the epidemic will unfold. The triggered
  lockdown watches instead, and needs a reliable, timely measurement of $I(t)$ — in
  practice the harder requirement, since surveillance reports cases late and
  incompletely. The observation-model session makes that gap explicit.
- The largest value of $I$ sits exactly at the trigger, not at a smooth top.
  Restrictions cut $\beta$ to $0.02$, which at $S = 782$ gives
  $\beta c S / N = 0.156$ against $\gamma = 0.25$, so $\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t$
  jumps straight from positive to about $-9.4$.
- $I$ stays continuous but its slope does not, so the curve turns a corner rather
  than arching over, and root-finding on $\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t = 0$ would find
  nothing. Whenever a parameter switches mid-run, the switching times matter as
  much as the callback's own events.
- Lifting the restrictions with `affect_neg!`, the third positional argument, does
  not work at this threshold. Imposing restrictions turns $I$ downward *at the
  same value of $I = 100$ that triggered them*, so the release condition is met
  at the root the solver has just handled; it does not re-detect an event it has
  just processed, and the restrictions never come off. The run above shows one
  event at day 11 and no release for the remaining 69 days.

The fix is **hysteresis**: two thresholds, plus a record of whether restrictions
are currently active. It imposes at $I = 100$, releases lower at $I = 60$, and
lets the condition watch whichever threshold currently applies.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch03-c2
restrictions_on = Ref(false)
policy_log = Tuple{Float64,Symbol}[]

# watch 100 while free, 60 while locked down
hysteresis_condition(u, t, integrator) =
    restrictions_on[] ? u[2] - 60.0 : u[2] - 100.0

function toggle_restrictions!(integrator)
    restrictions_on[] = !restrictions_on[]
    integrator.p = merge(integrator.p, (β = restrictions_on[] ? 0.02 : 0.05,))
    push!(policy_log, (integrator.t, restrictions_on[] ? :impose : :release))
end

sol_hyst = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5();
                 callback = ContinuousCallback(hysteresis_condition, toggle_restrictions!),
                 reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)

check("restrictions were imposed and then lifted", length(policy_log) == 2)
check("I never exceeded capacity",
      maximum(sol_hyst(t)[2] for t in tt) < 1.01 * capacity)

[(round(t; digits = 2), what) for (t, what) in policy_log]
```

- Restrictions go on at day 11.0 and come off at day 16.1, once prevalence has
  fallen to 60.
- The gap between the two thresholds is what stops the policy switching on and
  off repeatedly at a single value, and the `Ref` is what lets the condition
  remember which phase it is in.
- The epidemic does not return to 100 after release: by day 16 enough
  susceptibles have been infected that it cannot regrow that far.
